etymologies.etymologyHTML: From super- (prefix), from Middle English super-, from Latin super-, from super (“above”). Doublet of over and hyper.

definitions.definition: better than average, better than usual; wonderful.
(informal) Very; extremely (used like the prefix super-).

quote.citation: 1992 March 14, The Canberra Times, page 9, column 2:
quote.text: The job is super interesting for a person who enjoys a hardware environment and communicating with people.

quote.citation: 2022 November 18, Ryan Mac, Mike Isaac, Kellen Browning, quoting Elon Musk, “Elon Musk’s Twitter Teeters on the Edge After Another 1,200 Leave”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: “The best people are staying, so I’m not super worried,” he tweeted.

definitions.definition: (Australia, New Zealand, informal) Short for superannuation.

quote.citation: 1989, Kai Hwang, Doug DeGroot, Parallel processing for supercomputers and artificial intelligence:
quote.text: The performances and cost ranges of three classes of commercial supercomputers are given in Table 2.1. The full-scale supers are the most expensive class, represented by Cray, ETA, and Fujitsu systems, for example.

quote.citation: 1983, Sue Hubbell, A Country Year: Living the Questions, Boston, MA: Mariner Books, published 1999, →ISBN, page 69:
quote.text: There may be thirty to fifty supers in every outyard, and we have only about half an hour to get them off the hives, stacked and covered before the bees get really cross about what we are doing.

definitions.definition: (informal, US) Short for superintendent, especially, a building's resident manager (sometimes clarified as “building super”).
(neologism) Short for supernaturalist, especially as distinguished from bright.
Short for supernumerary; (theater) specifically, a supernumerary actor.

quote.citation: 1904–1905, Baroness Orczy [i.e., Emma Orczy], “The Affair at the Novelty Theatre”, in The Case of Miss Elliott, London: T[homas] Fisher Unwin, published 1905, →OCLC; republished as popular edition, London: Greening & Co., 1909, OCLC 11192831, quoted in The Case of Miss Elliott (ebook no. 2000141h.html), Australia: Project Gutenberg of Australia, February 2020:
quote.text: For this scene, a large number of supers are engaged, and in order to further swell the crowd, practically all the available stage hands have to ‘walk on’ dressed in various coloured dominoes, and all wearing masks.

quote.citation: 1916, Ring W. Lardner, “Three Kings and a Pair”, in The Saturday Evening Post‎[2]:
quote.text: The piece was gave by a bunch o’ supers the time I went. I’d like to see it with a real cast. They say it’s a whiz when it’s acted right.

quote.citation: 1973, Jeffrey Potter, Disaster by Oil, page 46:
quote.text: That is a lot of ship, about the size of big tankers before they grew so rapidly to become supers, mammoths and oilbergs.

quote.citation: 2009, James Robert Parish, Jim Henson, page 114:
quote.text: Supers are superimposed words that run across the TV screen and provide information such as the names of interview subjects. The newsroom sends a printed list of these supers to Perry.

quote.citation: 1917 Dadant, C. P., First Lessons in Beekeeping; revised & rewritten edition, 1968, by M. G. Dadant and J. C. Dadant, p 73:
quote.text: The question is: when is the best time to super?
Even running a supered "Re-enactment" caption for a few seconds is poor policy, he feels  […]
